stimulus.text: The engraving shows the Battle of Lexington on the morning of April 19, 1775. A long line of British regulars in red coats stands in formation across the town green, muskets level, firing a volley through a cloud of smoke. In the foreground, militiamen scatter and fall, and a few bodies lie on the ground. Behind the soldiers stand the houses of Lexington, including the meetinghouse. The engraving was made after Amos Doolittle's 1775 print of the battle.
stimulus.source_note: After Amos Doolittle, The Battle of Lexington, 1775. U.S. National Archives. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: Americans later called the first shot at Lexington “the shot heard round the world” because the clash

options.text: Was the largest battle of the Revolutionary War
options.misconception: Lexington was a small clash with eight colonists killed; the largest battles of the war came later and elsewhere.

options.text: Turned colonial resistance into open rebellion against Britain
Forced the British to evacuate Boston at once
options.misconception: The British stayed in Boston for nearly another year, until March 1776, so Lexington did not force them out.

options.text: Won the French alliance for the United States
options.misconception: France allied with the United States after Saratoga in 1778, not after Lexington in 1775.

rationales.B: Before Lexington the colonists resisted within the empire; after the shooting, they were in open rebellion, and the change echoed far beyond Massachusetts.
rationales.A: Lexington was tiny beside later battles like Saratoga and Yorktown; its importance was political, not military.
rationales.C: The British held Boston until March 1776, when cannon from Ticonderoga forced them out — not at Lexington.
rationales.D: The French alliance followed the American victory at Saratoga in 1777, three years after Lexington.
rationales.general:
1. Weigh the clash itself. Background: eight colonists died in minutes, and the British marched on — a small fight by any military measure.
2. Weigh what changed. Shooting at the king's troops crossed a line: resistance became rebellion, and there was no going back.
3. Check the later claims. Boston, Saratoga, and France all came later, so none of them explains the phrase.
Remember: a small event earns a large name when it changes what everyone is doing, not when it kills the most men.
